lines.text: Project time! You will make your own mini game, with AI as your coach and an honest log to prove it.
Choose a game you can finish in one class, like a number guessing game, a cricket quiz or a catch game in Scratch.
Small and working beats big and broken.
You can always add more later.
Write your idea and pseudocode first, and ask the AI to review the plan.
Build one step at a time and run it after each step.
Use your bug report template when something breaks.
Every time you use AI, write what you asked, what it said, and what you did with it.
Write down if its answer was wrong.
This log is part of your grade, so honesty earns marks.
At the end you will explain your code to the class or your teacher.
If there is a line you cannot explain, ask the AI to explain it and practise.
Your game, your code, your words.
Here are four mini games you can finish in one class, in Python or Scratch.
Pick one, or your own idea of the same size, and write it in one sentence.
Kabir asks the AI to explain one line of his guessing game.
The AI says the number twenty can never be picked, mixing it up with range.
Kabir tests it by printing the secret again and again, and twenty does appear.
He writes the catch in his what AI did log, which earns him marks.
A good log entry has four parts: what you asked, what it said, what you checked, and the result.
Notice that Kabir did not paste any AI code into his game.
Follow the route from idea to sharing, and keep your log open the whole time.
Your grade comes from the game, your testing, your honest log, and your explanation.
Great work! Let’s remember what we learned.
Now plan it, build it, test it, and share it!
